Sure... Random train of thoughts on markets now, optics like $LITE / memory + $IREN / Anthropic. 

On Memory: 

- Demand visibility on $MU / Samsung / SK Hynix extend into 2030-2031. 

Samsung has LTAs covering 70% of their capacity into 2031 (likely with SK Hynix type price floors)... and their operating profit is already absurd.  

There's a consensus that shortage in 2027 will be much more severe than 2026... Even $SNDK expends gross margins to exceed 80% entering 2030. 

You're going to hear Acer and other CEOs that want memory prices to go down cite bear cases like CXMT/YMTC, and Chinese players. 

But just looking at supply procurement that $NVDA is doing + hyperscalers, demand visibility is absurd for the next 5 years. And by that time, cumulative FCF coming in from these take/pay + pricing floor contracts might exceed some of their entire marketcaps so it feels like there's some baseline.  

Near-term is always volatile (IV dropped a ton across $EWY to $DRAM to $MU), so people with call options likely got nuked, along with underlying prices. 

But if Samsung is 3x 2027E, has 5 year LTAs with 70% of capacity committed from hyperscalers, and price floors, it's kinda hard to see these names suffer a sustained crash...   

For optics: 

- $LITE is literally sold out into 2029, starting discussions into 2030.  With demand visibility lasting into 2031… with hyperscalers largely funding the capacity buildout.  

Their 2028 Greensboro fab expansion was ~$5B in UHP laser capacity revenue alone, yet it’s basically allocated toward $NVDA (50%+ with options for more) and co from channel checks. 

Existing supply chain bottlenecks are extremely severe as optical content/XPU skyrockets entering 2027-2028.

So everything from DSPs/TIAs, photodiodes, lasers, InP/SOI substrates, wafers (epi, SOI, etc) are expected to go brrr. 

And what does that imply to anyone else with enormous amounts of capacity coming online like $AAOI + $SIVE + $MTSI capacity expansion in 2027? Or other players like Sumitomo / Furukawa? 

But again it's not quite the same situation as memory since the BOM % is extremely low in a cluster... If micron/samsung raised another 2000% hyperscalers would go bankrupt. But doing that for InP substrates seems possible. Or a 100% increase on CW laser content. 

I actually thought $LITE was overvalued at $100B+ MC, relative to capacity expansion on your smaller optical players to their respective MCs. So I chose to position accordingly (But lumentum does deserve premiums for demand visibility). 

For the companies leading the charge like $NVDA / $AVGO / $MRVL:

- Nvidia has 70% forward revenue growth FY2028 which is supply constrained growth. 
- Broadcom 100% Y/Y for 2027/2028 which is also supply constrained growth. 
- Marvell FY2031 upgraded guidance to $70B-$90B from $46B analyst projections... 

They all seem to be very happy.... and read through on demand for next 2-3 years is enormous (also echoing what $INTC CEO said today on the panel with $AVGO CEO).  

So you have overwhelming growth on memory + photonics + from the leaders... But the nuance is not everything in the AI supply chain get the same economic benefit. 

HBM/Laser/CPU/MLCC and other players in the bottlenecks look to be printing money. And seem to be the largest beneficiaries of the current bottlenecks. 

Test players are also getting price hikes + capacity allocated by players like $NVDA, but economic impact seems a tad lower than other players since forward P/E for many I modeled were still in the 45x+ range even if you hiked prices like 10-30%. 

As for capex intensive players... there's some like $IREN ($25-30B for 2027) that despite a deal with Anthropic ended up dropping.  I don't think markets seem to appreciate players spending a lot of money + ongoing financing (think they're like halfway through their $6B ATM). 

Just some hopium for $IREN investors, $NBIS also signed a deal with $META at the start of the year (but markets didn't care at all, since Nebius dropped to ~$70-80 at the lowest point?). 

But did 6 months later, as the time to revenue inflection gets closer and you're past the ATM/capex window, markets would likely care more. 

I don't think it's irrational but at the same time, the fundamentals have improved from Mirantis acquisition to others. I also think it was known for awhile it was either OpenAI/Anthropic from CEO comments earlier too? 

But either way to be a more risk-off environment where funds seem to be rotating to larger names as a flight to safety.

$CRWD / $PLTR  as just two example, but my take is that the valuations of these rotations are reaching clown levels. And that certain AI supply chain beneficiaries in comparison are undervalued now. 

I was thinking markets would just rotate to names that are extremely profitable like Samsung or names that have <2X P/E, so it was surprising to see $KOSPI and some legacy memory players get sold off today. 

Since all of this is colliding with uncertainty about sht macro environments and renewed sustainability concern of AI capex/commitments from frontier labs like OpenAI/Anthropic from due to that FT piece recently. I've always been sounding the alarm about the contractual backlog OpenAI has with $CBRS, $MSFT, $ORCL and others earlier in the year. But OpenAI did just raise $122B or so , so I don't quite think they're at risk of going down anytime soon. 

I also don't think overall capex can just exponentially go up, but even if it stalls / hovers around a certain point or even drops...

Capex toward certain areas like optics will still explode as hyperscalers fight over allocations when CPO scale up comes about, but might drop in others where more capacity comes online like test or DRAM. So it's a lot more nuanced than capex down = everything down or vice versa.   

I also slightly agree with community agreements that open weight models wouldn't lessen demand on AI infrastructure (otherwise $NVDA wouldn't be funneling funds into Reflection), but all the contractual obligations that Anthropic has might get messy if their models/company get cannibalized. 

Either way, I'd expect some of these frontier lab valuations to likely compress but I do think Jensen knows what he's doing though to avoid contagion.

But basically: 

- Extremely difficult market now, can't just throw money at any AI supply chain company like $GLW and expect it to go up. There's cause for concern of rate hikes mixed with financing per $AVGO CEO but not to the point you just blindly sell off everything.

Also I think markets are stupid and ties baskets together so that leads to mispricing + individual buying opportunities with certain chokepoints too.

If capacity + demand is visible and forward p/e compresses like $AAOI to single digits off hundreds or thousands of percent growth from hyperscalers off $471m transceiver revenues and hundreds of thousands of monthly ELSFP capacity. Or $SIVE coming online with 100M+ laser capacity + multiple foundries with ASP hikes on lasers. I wouldn't lump them into other AI supply chain names in IP like $RMBS or others. 

My take is that AI supply chain beneficiaries with closer inflection points, demand visibility, and forward P/E compressing due to economic leverage would likely outperform medium term despite current volatility. 

TLDR: 
- Memory strongest risk/adjusted return with LTAs + pricing floors extending to 2030's + buybacks. 
- My opinion is that optical supercycle for 2027-2028 with CPO/NPO is going to look absurd relative to capacity coming online of smaller suppliers. 
- Overwhelming fundamentals/growth colliding with sht macro + media scares
- Markets are stupid and groups things in baskets and sells them all off together or buys overvalued names, creating short/long opportunities

I'd give a prayer to people on short term options given underlying drop + IV decline, but there could be a reversal... who knows. Most valuable thing right now is time.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Meta $META unveiled Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, calling them its most capable AI models to date for personal AI agents and software development. Trained at Meta’s gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, the models combine Active Memory, which carries relevant context across conversations, with Active Focus, enabling agents to persist through complex tasks, explore alternative approaches, and confirm important actions with users. Meta said the models deliver state-of-the-art performance across agent, memory, and coding benchmarks, while supporting professional workflows involving software engineering, legal, financial, and health tasks. Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, while Muse Wonder Full is available to Muse Code subscribers and will also roll out to the Muse app, alongside stronger safeguards for privacy, malicious instructions, and misuse.

2. Broadcom $AVGO CEO Hock Tan warned that many investors are approaching AI like “casino gamblers,” arguing that capital is increasingly being deployed without a clear understanding of the industry's long-term economics. Tan said the next major constraint on AI may not be chips or power, but capital, as AI developers must prove they can generate sustainable returns from the enormous investments being made today. He also cautioned that some companies are overspending on AI initiatives and emphasized that long-term winners will be those that can turn AI deployments into profitable businesses rather than simply building larger models.

3. The S&P 500 $SPY traded just 18.3M shares today, marking its lowest full-session trading volume since December 26, 2003.

4. Market breadth continues to weaken even as the S&P 500 remains near record highs. 84% of S&P 500 stocks are now trading at least 10% below their all-time highs, despite the index sitting just 0.2% below its record close. Real Estate has been the weakest sector, with 97% of its stocks down at least 10%, followed by Materials (96%), Utilities (94%), and Consumer Discretionary (92%), while Energy (62%), Healthcare (70%), and Information Technology (72%) have held up relatively better. Overall, 59% of S&P 500 stocks are down at least 20% from their highs, 41% are down more than 30%, and 17% have fallen by 50% or more, highlighting the growing divergence between the index and the average stock.

5. Ondas $ONDS and Palantir $PLTR announced the launch of Regna AI, a new company focused on developing specialized AI models for governments and enterprises that want to retain full control over their models, data, and infrastructure. Initially wholly owned by Ondas, Regna will leverage Palantir’s AI platform and model-training infrastructure, with Ondas serving as its first customer. The company's initial focus is on intelligence, surveillance, and defense, developing AI models designed to run directly on drones, ground vehicles, and other edge hardware, even in environments with limited or intermittent connectivity. The companies said initial customer deployments are expected to begin over the coming months.

6. Since the start of 2024, a basket of 42 AI-related stocks has generated 67% of the S&P 500’s total price return, contributing roughly 22 percentage points of the index’s 33% gain over that period. By comparison, the remaining 458 companies have contributed just 11 percentage points. Those same AI leaders have also driven 58% of the S&P 500’s total earnings growth and 81% of all capital expenditure and R&D growth since the beginning of 2024, leaving the rest of the index responsible for only about 20% of investment growth. Meanwhile, just 29% of S&P 500 stocks have outperformed the index over the past 3 years, approaching the roughly 25% participation rate seen during the Dot-Com Bubble.

7. Google $GOOGL is simplifying the Gemini experience by moving toward a single prompt box with no modes or toggles, according to Google VP Josh Woodward. He said the goal is for users to simply tell Gemini what they want and have it automatically determine how to complete the task, reflecting a broader shift in AI user interfaces across the industry. Woodward also hinted that Google is building a “personal, proactive, powerful” version of Gemini, designed to leverage users’ Google data and work more intelligently across their digital lives. He added that Google has heard user requests to make Gemini work more seamlessly with the information they already store in Google services, saying “watch this space” as new capabilities are expected to launch soon.

8. Microsoft $MSFT CEO Satya Nadella announced the company's largest commitment yet to custom AI silicon, saying the Maia chip family will begin scaling to multi-gigawatt deployments starting next calendar year and become the primary inference platform for Microsoft's products and services. Microsoft also introduced Maia 300, which Nadella said delivers 40% more tokens per watt than leading GPU-based systems. The company is already deploying Maia 200 across the U.S., Europe, and Australia, achieving up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for workloads powering Teams and Copilot. Nadella said Microsoft's strategy is to continue improving full-stack efficiency while also incorporating the latest innovations from across the broader AI ecosystem.

9. Global physical gold-backed ETFs attracted a record $30.7B of inflows during Q3 2026, marking the largest quarterly inflow on record. September alone saw $10B of inflows, following $17.9B in August, the second-largest monthly inflow ever recorded. As a result, global gold ETF holdings increased by 67 tonnes in September to a record 4,256 tonnes, surpassing the previous high of 4,176 tonnes set in February. Year-to-date, gold ETFs have attracted $38.5B in inflows—equivalent to 226 tonnes of additional gold holdings—with demand positive across every region. UK-listed funds have led country-level inflows with $9.5B, overtaking China, highlighting exceptionally strong global demand for gold.

10. Anthropic said it has reduced the amount of data harvested through AI distillation attacks by approximately 90–99% after deploying new anti-distillation defenses. The company said Zhipu attempted to distill capabilities from Claude Fable 5, but switched to an older Claude model after encountering stronger cyber safeguards. Anthropic also revealed it has turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens' worth of paying traffic from suspected distillers, prioritizing model security over short-term revenue. The company said preventing unauthorized model distillation is a key national security issue, as frontier AI capabilities can otherwise be replicated at a fraction of the cost and integrated into foreign AI systems.

12. BlackRock has downgraded U.S. equities to Neutral while turning more constructive on U.S. Treasuries, according to a new outlook from the BlackRock Investment Institute and CIO Rick Rieder. The firm upgraded short-term Treasuries to Overweight, raised long-term Treasuries to Neutral from Underweight, and cut U.S. stocks to Neutral after maintaining an Overweight stance for an extended period. To every Democrat reading this. I'm not going to insult you. I'm going to run a simulation.

Start with the odds. The forecasts give your party roughly a 9 in 10 chance of taking the House on November 3rd, and a strong shot at the Senate. So let's assume you win. Here's what happens next.

January 2027. A new majority arrives in Washington with one obsession: the President. Subpoenas, hearings, impeachment talk. Meanwhile, the most important race in human history keeps running in the background. Superintelligence doesn't pause for a news cycle.

Every attempt at one simple national framework for AI dies in committee. The door opens wide for fifty state rulebooks written in Sacramento and Albany. Every startup now needs lawyers before engineers.

2027 to 2028. "Safety" becomes the word that justifies everything. Licenses for models above a certain size. Registries for compute. Mandatory guidelines on what models may and may not say, written by agencies nobody elected. Each rule sounds reasonable on its own. Together, they build a wall.

And here's the part nobody on your side wants to look at: who can climb that wall? Not the kid in Ohio with a laptop. Not the two-person startup in a garage. Only the handful of giants big enough to afford armies of compliance officers and lobbyists. Regulation doesn't kill monopolies. It crowns them.

If the White House follows, the loop closes. A few licensed labs, protected by the state, working hand in hand with agencies that decide what the models are allowed to think. Your search, your news, your doctor, your kid's tutor, your bank, all running on systems whose answers are shaped by a few officials and a few CEOs. Not because anyone is evil. Because that's what always happens when power and intelligence end up in the same hands.

That's not a fairer world. That's 1984 with a hyper-class on top. Not billionaires you can out-compete. A caste you can never join, because the door has been regulated shut.

That's the first branch.

The second branch is the optimistic one. They don't manage to capture it. Gridlock. Two years of hearings and vetoes. Nothing changes very deeply. But think about what "nothing changes" means in the decade where everything is changing. Every year of paralysis is a year where the future gets built somewhere else, by someone else, under someone else's values.

So the best case is lost time. The worst case is a permanent caste.

I know why you vote Democrat. You care about fairness. You hate oligarchy. You fear concentrated power. Good. So do I. That's exactly why I'm asking you to look at this. The most concentrated form of power ever created is about to exist. The only question is whether it stays spread across millions of builders, or gets handed to the state and the few companies it chooses to bless.

I'm writing from France, where the state already decided what we're allowed to build. Our best builders end up in San Francisco. Our politicians end up in committees.

You can still choose. Vote for the side that keeps the door open.

History is watching.

Yesterday I went through the replies under India's Olympic bid. Indians swimming in garbage. Cows on the running track. Men squatting on a race course. Most of it made by AI.

I wanted to know how this got so easy. The story starts in October 2022.

That month, Elon Musk bought Twitter. Within weeks, thousands of staff were gone. X later told Australia's online safety regulator it had cut 80% of its trust and safety engineers. The people whose job was to catch hate.

Researchers at UC Berkeley tracked what came next. Hate speech on the platform ran about 50% higher in the months after the takeover.

In January 2024, about 12,900 hate posts against South Asians in the US went up on X in a single month. That number comes from a report released two weeks ago by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate in Washington.

By the end of that year, X's own AI, Grok, could make any image in seconds. The report says AI is now mass producing cartoons of South Asians as dirty, as scammers, as vermin.

By June 2026, the monthly count had reached 43,800. Up 240%. The fastest growing kind called us dirty, up 171% in eighteen months. Almost half called us invaders or job thieves, with H1B at the centre.

And it does not stay online.

In July, Syed Sohail Uddin from Hyderabad was working at a mall kiosk in Utah. A man asked where he was from, then asked if he was Muslim. Then he stabbed him 15 times.

In September, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed at a Wyoming rest stop. Police have not named a motive. Sikh leaders say hate against Sikh truckers had been building online for months.

On October 2, someone threw bricks at a Swaminarayan temple in Ohio while priests and devotees were inside. It was the start of Hindu Heritage Month, days before Navratri.

Muslim. Sikh. Hindu. The hate does not ask which. It only sees an Indian.

Then came this month. Indians asked Musk simple questions about Starlink, and he called them Ambani's army of shills. The same week, the IOC confirmed India's 2036 bid. The replies filled up with AI cartoons. One had 198,000 likes.

India has problems. We know them, we fix them, and we talk about them louder than anyone.

America counted more than 7.7 lakh homeless people on a single night in 2024, the most ever. More than 1 lakh Americans died of drug overdoses in 2023. Indians don't fill American posts with AI cartoons of addicts in San Francisco. If we did, the world would call it racism. And it would be right.

This is not casual racism. It is organised. The report found accounts doxxing South Asians over H1B, influencers filming confrontations at their homes and offices, and AI cartoons pumped out faster than any human could draw.

And it runs on a platform that fired the people meant to stop it, built the tool that draws it, and carries it to millions. When the owner himself calls Indians shills, everyone below him gets the message.

I can't tell you what is in Elon Musk's head. I can only tell you what his platform allows.

He is fighting in public to sell Starlink to 140 crore Indians. He should look at what his own platform is selling about them.

This is where @plumenetwork stands out. 🪶

Plume is a public, EVM-compatible blockchain built to connect traditional finance with #DeFi not simply by tokenizing real-world assets, but by making them usable across the onchain financial ecosystem.

Think private credit, ETFs, commodities and other traditionally less accessible assets becoming composable financial building blocks. Assets that can be integrated into lending markets, used as collateral, traded, and incorporated into more advanced strategies.

This is the vision behind RWAfi.

🔹 An ecosystem built for adoption

Plume reports more than 200 protocols onboarded, while its testnet reached 18 million wallets and 280 million transactions. These figures highlight the scale of its testnet activity and ecosystem development, alongside partnerships involving institutions, distribution partners and asset managers.

🔹 Making RWAs useful beyond tokenization

The goal is to bring real-world assets into DeFi with utility. Depending on the asset, protocol and applicable requirements, users can stake, swap, lend, borrow and explore strategies that combine different onchain financial opportunities.

🔹 Connecting DeFi with institutional assets

Plume's vision includes bringing yield opportunities associated with asset managers and financial institutions such as #Superstate, #Apollo, #BlackRock, #Blackstone and #Invesco into the onchain ecosystem.

The key is understanding that these names represent the broader asset landscape Plume aims to connect with not a claim that every institution has a direct partnership with Plume or that every product is available to every user.

🔹 Composability changes the bigger picture

When tokenized assets can interact with lending protocols, serve as collateral and become part of structured financial strategies, their potential goes beyond simply representing ownership on a blockchain.

This opens the door to yield strategies, capital efficiency and new financial products while also introducing risks that depend on the underlying assets and protocols.

🔹 Beyond traditional asset classes

The RWAfi vision can extend to less conventional real-world assets, including GPUs, uranium, mineral rights and agricultural opportunities such as durian farms. These are examples of potential asset categories, not a guarantee that every category is currently available on Plume.

Plume's phased onboarding approach is designed to expand assets, integrations and use cases while addressing the needs of security, scalability and liquidity.

Traditional finance brings assets and capital.

plume:native is building infrastructure designed to bring these worlds together through a permissionless, transparent and demand-driven ecosystem.

I write copy for Shelby Sapp.

(ads, IG carousels, LinkedIn posts)

Here's how I write in her voice (as a 20 year old asian kid):

Step 1: Create a Story Bible

The first thing I do with every client is get FULL context on their entire life story. 

- What was their upbringing like?
- What motivates them?
- Why did they start doing what they do now?
- What were their mistakes?
- What are their biggest wins?
- What do they sell?
- What's their funnel?
- What are the things to avoid?
- Etc etc

You can't properly write for someone until you fully understand who they are and what they do.

Step 2: Set up a Voice Skill

The next step is to dissect their exact writing style so we can replicate it.

- I consume ALL of their content. Every single piece.
- I transcribe everything
- I feed it to Claude
- I analyze the patterns and create "rules"

When you create this skill, you need clear do's and don'ts, not vague instructions.

Step 3: Use an Anti-AI Checklist

Every LLM has AI-isms. Create a list of all of them. Tell it to check all of your writing for these and remove them before giving it back to you.

A few obvious ones:
- the “isn’t X, it’s Y” flip (both checklists put this #1)
- the “No X. No Y. Just Z.” tagline
- editorial wrap-up tags that start with “that’s the…” (that’s the trap, that’s the whole thing, that’s the point)
- empty decorative words (just, really, truly, genuinely, actually, simply, quietly, literally, very)
- overstatement/absolutes (whole, everyone, always, never, nobody, none of that)
- telling the reader how to feel instead of showing a concrete thing (stacked emotions like “same revenue, same guesswork, same nagging feeling”)
- “here’s the thing / here’s the kicker / here’s what nobody tells you” fake-suspense pivots

Hope this helps!

That story is now changing.

The country that once imported telecom equipment from Europe is now manufacturing advanced telecom hardware in India and sending it back to Europe.

This is not merely a manufacturing milestone. It signals a fundamental shift in India's position within the global technology supply chain.

And the transformation is not happening because India is simply assembling imported parts.

Ericsson's expanding Indian R&D footprint reinforces that shift. Thousands of engineers are working in India on advanced telecommunications technologies, while Bengaluru has become an important centre for telecom research and engineering.

India's enormous 5G market has naturally played a major role.

With hundreds of millions of 5G subscriptions and rapidly increasing data consumption, India is no longer just a customer for telecom companies. It is one of the world's most important environments for deploying, scaling and developing next-generation connectivity.

Government policy has also helped accelerate this transformation, particularly through production-linked incentives aimed at strengthening domestic telecom and networking-equipment manufacturing.

At the same time, global companies are actively diversifying their supply chains.

The era of depending overwhelmingly on a single manufacturing geography is increasingly being replaced by a strategy built around resilience, diversification and trusted production centres.

India is positioning itself directly in that transition.

And the implications extend beyond antennas.
